title: Elastic Compute, Containers & Serverless Workloads
summary: Compare Virtual Machines, Containers (Docker/Kubernetes), and Serverless execution trade-offs including cold starts, state isolation, and auto-scaling.
learningObjectives: Evaluate VM hypervisors vs Linux container namespaces vs serverless micro-VMs
Design stateless application instances backed by shared caches and databases for horizontal scaling
prerequisiteConcepts: Understanding of IaaS vs PaaS boundaries

sections.heading: 1. Virtual Machines vs Containers vs Serverless Micro-VMs
sections.content:
Every VM packages an entire guest Operating System kernel atop hardware virtualization (hypervisor), consuming gigabytes of RAM and tens of seconds to boot. Containers share the host Linux kernel while isolating processes cleanly via namespaces and resource cgroups, yielding lightweight sub-second startup and identical environments from developer laptops to production nodes.

Serverless functions (e.g., AWS Lambda via Firecracker micro-VMs) abstract server capacity completely behind event invocations, billing strictly per millisecond executed—ideal for spiky HTTP hooks and async workers, though stateful long-running sockets fit containers/VMs cleanly.

codeExamples.code:
[VM Model]             [Container Model]        [Serverless Model]
App A  | App B         App A  | App B           Fn Handler (Event)
Bins   | Bins          Bins   | Bins            Isolated Micro-VM
Guest  | Guest         Container Runtime        Provider Runtime
---Hypervisor---       ----Host Linux Kernel--- Provider Control Plane
Physical Hardware      Infrastructure VMs       Billed per 1ms Execution
codeExamples.explanation: Abstraction reduces OS overhead as you move from dedicated Guest VMs to shared-kernel Containers and event-driven Serverless functions.

keyPoints: Always build stateless compute nodes: keep user sessions in Redis/JWTs rather than local `/tmp` disk.
Multi-stage Docker builds keep runtime images minimal and free of compilers or credentials.
commonMistakes: Storing uploaded user images or login sessions on VM local disk, which disappears when Auto Scaling replaces or terminates an instance.

sections.heading: 2. Graceful Container Packaging & Health Check Probes
sections.content: Production compute targets rely on explicit container health endpoints (`/healthz`) and non-root execution UIDs so orchestrators detect stalled workers early and drain requests cleanly before replacing pods.

codeExamples.code:
# Hardened Multi-Stage Dockerfile (Zero build tools in production runtime)
FROM node:22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S appgrp && adduser -S appusr -G appgrp
USER appusr
COPY --from=builder /app/.next ./.next
COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules ./node_modules
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/health || exit 1
CMD ["npx", "next", "start"]
codeExamples.explanation: Switching to `USER appusr` prevents root container privilege escalation while multi-stage copying strips compilers from the runtime image.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Lean non-root production image verified via healthcheck probe

keyPoints: Stateless containers enable horizontal Auto Scaling behind Load Balancers.
Expose `/healthz` readiness checks and respect `SIGTERM` for graceful draining.
commonMistakes: Running production web apps inside containers as default `root` UID 0.

exercises.title: Compute Workload Right-Sizing & Dockerfile Review
exercises.objective: Eliminate root execution and stateful storage bugs from a container deployment.
exercises.description: Inspect a deployment writing user PDF uploads directly into VM `/var/uploads` inside a root container. Refactor the architecture for horizontal multi-AZ auto-scaling.
instructions: Explain what happens to `/var/uploads` if the Auto Scaling group scales down by 1 instance.
Replace local disk file storage with signed S3 object uploads.
Update the Docker runtime configuration to execute under a non-root service user.

exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.

Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Moving uploads to object storage (S3), state to Redis/DB, and processes to non-root UIDs makes compute truly elastic and fault-tolerant.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What happens if an auto-scaled web server saves uploaded user avatars onto its local EC2 instance disk?

options.text: Files vanish when instances scale down or get replaced, and other balanced instances cannot serve those files
Docker copies files across regions in 1ms
Load balancers store binary files inside headers

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Local disks on auto-scaled nodes are ephemeral and node-bound; durable shared assets belong in Object Storage (S3/GCS).

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why do multi-stage Dockerfiles produce cleaner, safer cloud images?

options.text: Compilers and dev caches stay isolated in the build stage and are omitted from the lean runtime container
They allow root SSH access directly from browsers
They skip TLS verification on registries
They bundle entire VM hypervisors inside containers

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Smaller runtime images transfer faster across clusters and reduce exposed software CVEs.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When is a Serverless function (Lambda / Cloud Functions) generally LESS appropriate than containers/VMs?

options.text: Sustained CPU-saturated rendering jobs running continuously for hours or requiring persistent raw WebSockets
Asynchronous thumbnail generation on S3 image upload

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Continuous compute-saturated workloads and persistent long-lived stateful protocols are often cheaper and better served on containers/VMs.

recap: You contrasted VMs, containers, and serverless models and built stateless multi-stage non-root workloads.
